title: The robot's cartwheel was a human's first

beats: This robot just did a cartwheel. A human did it first.
Researchers at Berkeley and Stanford gave a Unitree G1 humanoid about two and a half hours of human motion capture. Walking, running, dancing, martial arts, cartwheels.
It doesn't copy frame by frame. A reward system scores how closely it tracks the move, and punishes jerky motion, unsafe joints, and bumping into itself.
Two AI models compress those moves into a compact code, then plan new sequences from it. Sprints. Spin kicks. Aerial cartwheels.
Thirty clips ran on the real robot. Joystick control and obstacle avoidance worked without retraining.
Does it look human? Seventy-seven people compared its walking and running with Unitree's standard controller. In seventy point eight percent of comparisons, the new one looked more natural.
Boston Dynamics and the RAI Institute built a similar system, ZEST. It learns from mocap, video, or animator keyframes. About ten hours of training, one GPU.
The catch, per ZEST's authors: flat, non-slippery floors only, and no moves it hasn't seen.
Every robot flip starts as someone's dance. Whose motion is it? Tell me below. Follow for the next AI story.
